title: Anchor — October 2026
coverLines: Habits that hold — when life won't
Five small anchors for a single-parent home
One ask instead of ten
summary: Anchor's October guide for single-parent households: habits small enough to survive the hard weeks — five minutes, one ask, routines that hold, rest that protects and grace for the missed day.

blocks.text: October has five weeks, so here are five habits — one a week. Each week opens with a verse to pray (`Pray it`), a short reflection, and a `Do it` list. This guide is written for strength that is already stretched, so every habit is deliberately small. Keep week one, or keep all five — but never keep the guilt. Grace isn't a separate week; it's the water every week swims in.
The habit of the lighthouse keeper

The lighthouse keeper doesn't command the sea. He keeps one small light burning through the storm, every night, when every sensible person has gone to bed. That is the whole job — one small thing, repeated — and it is what keeps the whole coastline safe. On the noisy, exhausting nights, remember: you are not failing because the storm is loud. Holding one small habit is the entire assignment.

Parenting alone runs on hundreds of tiny repetitions: breakfast, school run, homework, bedtime, laundry, and then it starts again. This month we turn five of them into anchors — things that hold you and your children steady, even when the week dips.
God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble.

Five minutes before anyone else is awake. A breath, a verse, one honest sentence to God about the day coming. Five minutes will not fix the roof or the timetable, but it drops a small anchor into the morning before the morning decides for you. On the days five minutes won't happen, take ninety seconds. Anchor beats zero.

blocks.caption: Five minutes before anyone is awake — anchor beats zero.

items: Set out a verse card and a glass of water the night before
Take five minutes before the house wakes — even on the school run
Mark the days you kept it; don't count the ones you didn't

blocks.text: Week 2 — Routines that survive a bad week
But everything should be done in a fitting and orderly way.

Pick three routines that make a bad week survivable: a fixed bedtime, breakfast ready the night before, and one load of washing on the same day every week. Nothing more. Three anchors beat thirty intentions on the weeks when the tyre goes flat and the fever arrives. Order is a mercy, not a measure of worth.

blocks.caption: Three anchors beat thirty intentions.

items: Choose your three: bedtime, breakfast, washing-day — only three
Move any two of them to 'the night before'
Watch the school calendar and loop in the village for the heavy week

blocks.text: Week 3 — One ask instead of ten
Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

The single-parent habit that feels hardest: asking. The village is real — the relief, the church, the driving rota — but it can't respond to a generalised cry for help. It responds to one specific person asked one specific thing. 'Can you take Tuesday?' beats 'we're struggling'. Practise the habit by asking small, and ask one person, not everyone.

blocks.caption: One person, one specific ask — the village responds to specifics.

items: Write down one specific need and one specific person who can fill it
Ask them this week — a sentence, not a paragraph
Say yes when someone else needs the same from you

blocks.text: Week 4 — The bedtime that protects you
In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me dwell in safety.

Your children sleep because you guard the boundary. But who guards yours? A fixed wind-down — screens parked, an alarm, a truthful 'the day is done' — is not a luxury on a stretched schedule; it's the anchor that keeps the one holding the anchor from drowning. The bedtime that protects you is part of the routine that protects them.

blocks.caption: Guard your wind-down — it's part of protecting them.

items: Set a phone-off alarm 60 minutes before you intend to sleep
Name one screen that stays out of the bedroom
Thank God out loud for one good thing from the day, then close it

blocks.text: Week 5 — Grace for the missed day
My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.

The fifth habit is the one that makes the other four human: when you miss, you don't double up and you don't spiral. Stacked guilt is heavier than any missed day. The anchor habit is not never dropping — it's dropping, picking the rope back up tomorrow, and letting God be sufficient for the day you dropped.

blocks.caption: Missed days are part of the pattern — grace is the habit that repeats.

items: If you miss a day, do NOT do two days' worth in one
Say the honest sentence: 'today was a drop day — tomorrow is normal'
Let someone in the village know your rhythm this month
Which of the five anchors did your week most need?
What is the one ask you've been carrying alone — and who could carry half?
Where do you quietly wait to be superhuman? What would change if you didn't?
Who in the village needs the lift your habit could be to them?

title: Base — October 2026
coverLines: Five habits that build a house
The daily ten · the weekly date · money without the fight
Small routines, a steady home
summary: Base's October guide for couples: a daily ten-minute check-in, a weekly phone-off date, money talk that doesn't fight, the apology habit and praying together — the small repetitions a house is built on.

blocks.text: October has five weeks, so here are five habits — one a week. Each week opens with a verse to pray (`Pray it`), a short reflection, and a `Do it` list. These are for couples and those building toward a covenant: one small repetition at a time, done together, until the house is built.

A house is not built in the architect's drawing — it's built in the thousands of unglamorous flicks of a trowel. And yet no one walks through a solid home wishing the bricklayer had been more exciting. Couples who last are not the ones with the loudest romance; they are the ones who kept laying bricks — the daily ten, the weekly date — long after the excitement moved out and quietly moved back in.

Marriage runs on habit the way a house runs on foundations — invisible, load-bearing, holding everything above it. This month we lay five small habits. None of them is dramatic. All of them are structural.
Therefore encourage one another and build each other up.

Ten minutes a day — after work, before the evening runs away with you — with the phones in another room. Not to fix anything, not to manage the calendar: just to be un-sorted people together for a moment. Most couples don't grow apart in a season; they drift apart in the ten minutes every night that belonged to nobody.

blocks.caption: Ten minutes that belong to nobody else.

items: Fix ten minutes a day — same time, same sofa, no screens
One rule: not a debrief of the whole day, just 'how are you, really?'
Let each of you answer before either of you fixes

blocks.text: By wisdom a house is built, and through understanding it is established.

Base's week, on a month of habits: one fixed, low-cost, phone-off evening a week. It doesn't need to cost money — a walk, a potluck movie, childcare-swap even better. The date is the smallest habit in the month and the one the whole house quietly depends on. Book it like an appointment, because the marriage is one.

blocks.caption: The weekly date — the smallest habit the whole house depends on.

items: Put one fixed evening in the shared calendar — non-movable
Low-cost and phone-off: walk, cook, or the second-hand movie night
Mention it this week to a closer couple — swap childcare and make it monthly

blocks.text: Week 3 — Money talk without the fight
Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.

Most money fights are not about money — they're about being in different rooms of the same country and not knowing it. One Saturday a month, same script: what came in, what went out, and one goal we both actually want. It's a team meeting, not a tribunal. The marriage can survive a bad month far better than it can survive money that never gets discussed.

blocks.caption: Same Saturday, same script — a team meeting, not a tribunal.

items: Fix one shared 30 minutes this month — a Saturday, not a tired Tuesday
Use the script: in, out, and the one goal we're both for
End by agreeing the single number you'll both move — no ambushes

blocks.text: Bear with each other and forgive one another.

A good apology is fast, specific and aimed at the wound, not the crowd: 'I was impatient when you — and I was wrong.' Not 'I'm sorry you got upset.' The apology habit keeps small cracks from becoming load-bearing fractures. Never sleep storing up a list of the other's faults; that list is a building that will eventually fall on you both.

blocks.caption: Fast, specific, aimed at the wound — cracks cleaned before they bear weight.

items: Apologise within the same day, every time — even when it's 'small'
Make it specific: name the moment and the wrong, not 'everything'
Say 'I forgive you' out loud when you receive one — it seals the repair

blocks.text: For where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them.

One sentence each, every night, out loud. It doesn't need to be eloquent and it doesn't need to be long. Couples who pray together stop being co-managers of a household and become two knees under the same roof — and a house with that foundation doesn't just resist the storm; it is where the storm's neighbours come to shelter.

blocks.caption: One sentence each — two knees under the same roof.

items: At the end of the daily ten, one sentence each — that's it
Keep it honest: thanks, a need, a fear — not a performance
Mention it in the relationship group; you'll be surprised who's doing it already
Which of the five felt hardest to say out loud this month?
Where in your week does the ten minutes currently belong to nobody?
What is one money conversation you've both been circling? Sat down and take the script with you.
Whose 'I forgive you' have you been waiting to hear — or to say?

title: Footsteps — October 2026
coverLines: Ben Franklin built himself — one morning at a time
Study · work · save · rest
The habits that build the build-you-need years
summary: October's guide for Surge and Pulse: five habits from the industry of the sixteen-to-thirty-three years — study, work, saving, rest and a rhythm that holds them all.

blocks.text: October has five weeks, so here are five habits — one a week. Each week opens with a verse to pray (`Pray it`), a short reflection, and a `Do it` list. You're not building five habits in one month; you're trying five and keeping the ones that hold.
The habit of the man with the list

Benjamin Franklin kept a ledger of virtues — thirteen of them — and each week he focused on one, marking his failures like someone balancing a budget. The famous autobiography he wrote in 1791 is less a memoir than a case study: a young man who decided to build himself the way you build a trade, one small daily practice at a time. He was not the cleverest man in the room. He was the one with the systems.

blocks.caption: A ledger of habits — Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography (1791), public domain.

blocks.text: This is the season of life where every decision echoes for a decade. Habits are how you stack the small wins into something that outlasts motivation. Keep it boring. Boring habits win.
Satisfy us in the morning with your unfailing love, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days.

Franklin began every day by asking 'What good shall I do this day?' The first hour decides the next ten. A fixed morning — water, one verse, one direction — is the cheapest investment in the whole day you can make.

blocks.caption: Win the first hour and the day follows.

items: Wake at a fixed time every day this week
Before your phone: one verse, one glass of water, one 'today I will'
Ask Franklin's question — 'What good shall I do this day?'

blocks.text: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.

Surge's term theme, in one verse. The approved worker studies. Whether it's a trade, a subject or Scripture, thirty minutes a day compounds absurdly over a year. Show up to the page and let the habit carry the ambition.

blocks.caption: Thirty minutes a day, shown up — the study habit compounds.

items: Block one fixed 30-minute study slot for five days
Same place, same chair, phone in another room
End each session by writing one line: 'I can now…'

blocks.text: Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank.

Pulse's whole message is that skill outranks luck. The Launch Pad and Hustle Hub exist to put your work in front of people who will promote it. Show up on time, finish the thing, do the boring part properly — and let your work speak.

blocks.caption: The Launch Pad work day — show up, build, become.

items: Do the hardest task first each day — the one you avoid
Name one piece of work you keep 'almost done' and finish it
Bring your work to a mentor or peer and ask for honest feedback

blocks.text: The wise store up choice food and oil, but fools gulp theirs down.

The Pulse Wallet method in one verse: pay yourself first. Money moves the moment it arrives — if you don't move it somewhere first, something else will. Save before you spend, however small, and let the habit do the growing no one notices at the time.

blocks.caption: Move money somewhere safe before anything spends it.

items: Set up an automatic transfer the day pay lands — even R50
Track one week of spending in a notes app — no judgement
Write the one thing you're saving for; name it out loud

blocks.text: Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, 'Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.'

Busy work isn't healthy work. Rest is not the absence of habits — it's one of the habits. A rhythm of honest work and honest rest is what keeps the other four going for the whole decade, not just the month.

blocks.caption: Rest without guilt — rest is part of the habit.

items: Guard one full screen-free evening this week
Sleep a fixed seven-plus hours — track it like a quota
On Sunday, thank God for the work that's done and let the undone wait
Which of the five did you actually try? What made it stick or slip?
Where is your life most 'gulped down' — the thing that needs moving first?
Who do you want holding you accountable to the one you keep? Name them, this week.

title: Hearth — October 2026
coverLines: The mother who prayed under her apron
A small fidelity keeps a whole house
Five habits for the heart of the home
summary: October's guide for Nexus families: five home habits from the faithfulness of Susannah Wesley — prayer, morning anchors, the date habit, small savings and table grace.

blocks.text: Hearth is the magazine for the heart of the home — families building a house where faith is caught as much as taught. October has five weeks and five habits, one a week. Each week opens with a verse to pray (`Pray it`), a short reflection, and a `Practice it` list. Go gently; one kept habit outshines five abandoned ones.
The habit of the mother with the apron

Susannah Wesley raised nineteen children in one house, and her secret was famously small. When the press of family life grew too loud, she would throw her apron over her head. The children learned that mother was speaking to God and was not to be disturbed — and in that strange, wonderful signal, a whole generation learned what prayer was for. Two of her sons, John and Charles, helped turn a continent toward faith. It began under an apron, in a kitchen, as a habit nobody thought to write down.

blocks.caption: The kitchen habits outlast the ones we stage and announce.

blocks.text: October — habits that hold a house
A home is a collection of tiny repeated moments. Change the moments and you change the house. This month we plant five small ones — the kind a busy family can actually keep.

Susannah fixed a daily time to talk with God — not when it was convenient, but when she decided. A family faithful to one set prayer time — even ten minutes — gives the house a heartbeat that survives the chaos of the rest of the day.

blocks.caption: A fixed time to talk with God — the house has a heartbeat.

items: Fix one daily prayer time — after supper, before school, whenever holds
Keep it short: one thanks, one need, one 'help us today'
Let the smallest member of the family lead it once

blocks.text: He wakens me morning by morning, wakens my ear to listen like one being instructed.

Faith is caught in the mornings before anyone is watching. One verse read at breakfast, one prayer said over the school run — the small anchor that keeps the family boat in place through the day's weather. It needn't be long. It must be daily.

blocks.caption: Anchor the day before the day starts moving.

items: Read one verse together at breakfast every day this week
Say the school-run prayer — 'God, go with them' — out loud
Write the verse on the fridge so the habit has a home

blocks.text: Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain.

Healthy marriages build healthy families, and healthy marriages are built by small, regular attention — not occasional grand gestures. A fixed weekly date — low-cost, childcare-swapped, put in the calendar like a non-negotiable — is a habit the whole house benefits from.

blocks.caption: A fixed date protects the house God is building.

items: Put one date night in the calendar this week — non-negotiable
Swap childcare with another family if you need to
Turn the phones off for the evening, together

blocks.text: Whoever gathers money little by little makes it grow.

Wisdom loves the small and faithful. A family that saves a little every week — however modest — is building a wall against the emergencies that sink households. The jar, the envelope, the standing order: all of them are just faithfulness made visible.

blocks.caption: Little by little — faithfulness made visible.

items: Open a savings rhythm — any amount, the same day every week
Let the children see it happen and know what it's for
Name the goal: 'one month of groceries safe' is enough to start

blocks.text: Taste and see that the Lord is good.

Everything meets at the table. A grace said before the meal — short, real, unpolished — tells every child that food is a gift and that Someone is listening. It is the smallest habit in this guide and, in its quiet way, the one the house remembers longest.

blocks.caption: Short, real, unpolished — grace at the table.

items: Say grace at every meal this week — one sincere sentence is enough
Hold hands if that feels right; don't if it doesn't
Let each family member thank God for one specific thing

blocks.text: Talk it over — around the table

items: Which habit does our home already have, and which one do we most need?
Where does our family need an 'apron moment' — a time not to be disturbed for God?
What's one small thing we'll still be doing this time next month?

title: Prime — October 2026
coverLines: Prime isn't an age — it's a mindset
Five habits that keep the years working for you
Morning · open doors · give · rest · review
summary: Prime's October habits guide: a non-negotiable morning, doors that open to neighbours, the rhythm of giving, rest as stewardship and a monthly review that keeps the decades compounding.

blocks.text: October has five weeks, so here are five habits — one a week. Each week opens with a verse to pray (`Pray it`), a short reflection, and a `Do it` list. Prime is where habits have already had years to compound — the goal this month is to make sure the account keeps earning, for you and for everyone coming up behind you.
The habit of the long game

Money compounds because the person managing it reviews it regularly and refuses to touch it. A life compounds the same way. Prime's habit is the quarterly review, the monthly review, the daily non-negotiable — an investor who keeps auditing the portfolio of the years, adding what is good and cutting what quietly drains. You don't need a loud decade; you need a compounding one.
This month's habits are the ones that keep the years working for you — and for the generations who will use your momentum as their starting line.
In the morning, Lord, you hear my voice; in the morning I lay my requests before you and wait expectantly.

The day's first conversation belongs at the top of the ledger: prayer before the news, before the phone, before the demands of others get first claim on your attention. A fixed morning hour is the habit the other four lean on. If the schedule flexes, the hour flexes with it — but never the direction: firstfruits, then the rest.

blocks.caption: Firstfruits of the day — before the phone gets his say.

items: Fix one morning hour and guard it from the overflow of the night before
Pray your requests before you read a single headline
Write one line: who in your life is the day's first person to serve

blocks.text: Do not forget to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have shown hospitality to angels without knowing it.

Prime's month of open doors: the Elders' Table hosting the wider family, Legacy Lab mentors matched to Surge and Pulse. The door habit is one invitation a month — a coffee window open, a courtyard chair pulled out, a table with one empty seat. Your years of habits are about to become someone else's shortcut.

blocks.caption: One invitation a month — an open door is the whole gospel in one action.

items: Invite someone specific to the next Elders' Table or Prime Circle
Keep one door — literal — open for an hour of 'drop-ins welcome'
Turn one offer you'd make vaguely into a named, dated one

blocks.text: In everything I did, I showed you that by this kind of hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words the Lord Jesus himself said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'

Give first, on a fixed rhythm — not 'when I have margin'. The giving habit is financial (automated, firstfruits) and it is personal (mentorship, Legacy Lab time). You have spent decades accumulating exactly what someone twenty years behind you cannot buy: the shortcut only experience can sell.

blocks.caption: The shortcut only experience can sell — give it away.

items: Check your giving is automated — if not, set it this week
Book one hour to mentor or be in a Legacy Lab matching conversation
Give someone the exact lesson that cost you the most to learn

blocks.text: He makes me lie down in green pastures, he leads me beside quiet waters, he refreshes my soul.

Rest is not the absence of stewardship; it is one of the assignments. The body and the schedule are trusts — sleep, walking, health checks and a sabbath that isn't optional. Prime is not a description of exhaustion. The person who keeps pouring from an empty well ends the years handing out an apology instead of a legacy.

blocks.caption: Green pastures are an assignment, not a reward for later.

items: Book the health check you've postponed — this month, not 'one day'
Guard one weekly rhythm that genuinely rests you, and name it
Put one green-pasture walk in the shared calendar and keep it

blocks.text: Let us examine our ways and test them, and let us return to the Lord.

One still hour at the end of the month, with the ledger open before the Lord: what did I do, what did I pour, who did I serve, and what one thing changes next month? The monthly review is where a compounding life is actually audited. A life that is never reviewed is a life being spent by whoever got to it first.

blocks.caption: The monthly review — audit the portfolio of the years.

items: Set one hour on the last Sunday of the month — same time as giving-day
Four questions: did I do, did I pour, who did I serve, what changes
Pray through it before you change a single habit — let the Spirit edit first
Which of the five is already running on autopilot — and which needs the review?

title: Pulse — October 2026
coverLines: Five habits that move the needle
Money Monday · the craft hour · one connection
Small systems, loud results
summary: Pulse's October habits guide: Money Monday, a weekly hour of craft, one real connection, one unplanned hour of margin and firstfruits — the small systems that build a life loud enough to be heard.

blocks.text: October has five weeks, so here are five habits — one a week. Each week opens with a verse to pray (`Pray it`), a short reflection, and a `Do it` list. You're not adopting five habits in a month; you're trying five and keeping the ones that hold. Start with week one and go.
The habit of the person who got ready

Nobody notices the hours before the spotlight. Expertise isn't a talent lottery — it's repetition with a system. The person who shows up to the same hour of craft, the same week, the same month, ends the year two hundred hours ahead of the one who keeps promising to 'get serious' someday. Pulse habits aren't about being seen. They're about being ready when the room finally turns to look.

Every one of this month's habits is a system, not a mood. A system works when you don't. Automate the boring parts, guard the non-negotiable hour, and let the repetition do the growth no one notices at the time.
Be sure you know the condition of your flocks, give careful attention to your herds.

Most money chaos is not a spending problem — it's an awareness problem. Fifteen minutes every Monday to look at the numbers you moved and the numbers you let move you turns a blur of anxiety into a ledger you actually manage. Same day, same hour, no judgement.

blocks.caption: Fifteen minutes with the numbers — not a scolding, an audit.

items: Block 15 minutes on Monday — the same time every week
Write down what moved: in, out, and what's left
Name the one number you'll move this week, and move it

blocks.text: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might.

One unbroken hour a week on the skill that will outrank the competition. Same place, same chair, phone in another room, doing the hardest part — not the satisfying part. The Launch Pad and Hustle Hub give you the room; the hour is yours.

blocks.caption: The craft hour — the hardest problem, not the fun one.

items: Book one 60-minute block for the skill that pays your future
Pick the hardest 45 minutes, not the flashy 45
End the hour with one line: 'today I can now…'

blocks.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.

Networking isn't events — it's one meaningful conversation a week. Coffee with someone ahead of you, a walk with someone beside you, a message to someone behind you. One real connection beats forty business cards. The network night is where you keep it warm; the weekly habit is where it grows.

blocks.caption: One table, one conversation — connections are a habit.

items: Invite one person to coffee or a call — not a group message
Go with one genuine question, not an elevator pitch
Send a follow-up within 24 hours: one line that proves you listened

blocks.text: Be still, and know that I am God.

The busiest people don't have the best instincts — they're just loudest about being busy. One unplanned hour a week, and do not fill it. No agenda, no feed, no 'productive' use. Creativity and clear thinking grow in the empty hour, the way crops grow in fallow land.

blocks.caption: An unplanned hour — do not schedule it, do not fill it.

items: Guard one hour with no plan and no phone
Leave the to-do list in the other room
Follow the boredom — that's where the good idea is hiding

blocks.text: Honor the Lord with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops.

The habit that holds all the others: give to God before anything else gets first claim. Firstfruits means the giving is automatic as the money arrives — an instruction from its first cent. Same automation you use for saving, pointed at the kingdom. It orders every other number on the page.

blocks.caption: Firstfruits — the giving that goes out before the rest of the list.

items: Set giving to move automatically on payday, before saving
Write down where your firstfruits go — church, mission, mercy
Tell your partner-in-the-habit, so the instruction can't be reversed by a bad week
Which of the five became a system already — and which one fought you?
Where is your money 'unseen' — the number most likely to surprise you?
Who is one connection you keep meaning to make? Name them and book it this week.
What would change if you gave before you spent?

title: Relate — October 2026
coverLines: Daniel kept his window open and his knees bent
Five habits that grow a whole family
Screen-free hour — one week to try it
summary: October's family guide: five habits around one table — prayer at meals, a verse on the wall, kindness between siblings, a screen-free hour and a gratitude jar that fills a house.

blocks.text: This is the family issue of Relate — five habits, one a week, that a whole household can grow together. Each week opens with a verse to pray (`Pray it`), a short reflection, and a small `Do it` list for the week. Pick the one habit that fits your season and go gently.

Daniel never closed the window. Three times a day he knelt and prayed toward Jerusalem — not because a law told him to, but because the habit had already decided for him. When the law finally tried to stop him, his knees were already bent. Habits are how faithfulness survives the seasons when keeping it gets expensive.
Now Daniel… got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.
October — habits that grow a family

A family habit is a promise a whole household keeps until it keeps them. This month we plant five — one verse and one small practice for every week. You don't need to do all five. Even one, done together, changes the weather of a home.
Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.

The table is where most of your family's life already happens. Add a single sentence of thanks before the first mouthful, and the meal becomes a little altar. Start with one word — grateful, brave, tired, safe — and let the prayer grow as the habit does.

blocks.caption: One sentence before the first mouthful — a little altar, three times a day.

items: Say one word of thanks before every meal this week
Let each person (shortest to tallest) pick the word on their night
On Friday, read a verse at dinner — the table is a good pulpit

blocks.text: Week 2 — A verse for the wall
These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children.

What hangs on your wall teaches your children what your house believes. One verse, written out and taped where everyone walks past, becomes the soundtrack of the hallway. It does the teaching on the days you're too tired to.

blocks.caption: A verse on the wall is a habit your house keeps for you.

items: Pick a house verse and write it out by hand
Tape it where everyone passes twice a day — mirror, fridge or door
Recite it to each other at dinner on Sunday

blocks.text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

The loudest classroom in the family is the sibling one. Kindness between brothers and sisters is a habit — you do the gentle thing first, and the feeling follows later. One gentle answer can stop a whole evening from tipping over.

blocks.caption: Gentle answers are a habit siblings grow together.

items: Start each day asking one sibling 'what's one good thing you need today?'
A gentler first sentence: try 'can we try again?' instead of the sharp one
Catch someone being kind and say it out loud

blocks.text: There is a time for everything, and a season for every activity under the heavens.

The loudest habit in most homes is the phone. One hour a day with every screen in a drawer restores the space where people actually look at each other — and the space where faith is caught, not taught. Start with dinner.

blocks.caption: One hour with screens in a drawer — room for each other again.

items: Pick one hour a day — dinner is the classic — and park every phone
Put a bowl at the door; the phones sleep there till the hour is done
Fill the hour with one slow thing: a walk, a game, a chapter

blocks.text: This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.

Thanks is the quickest way to reorder a difficult day. Two thanks at dinner, every night, dropped into a jar — and by the 31st you have a family history of God's faithfulness, written by the people who lived it.

blocks.caption: Two thanks a night fills a jar — and a family's memory of God.

items: Set a jar and a stack of slips by the supper spot
Every night, everyone writes or says two thanks
On 31 October, read the jar out loud around the table

blocks.text: Talk it over — as a family

items: Which of the five habits did our home need most — and why?
What would Daniel's window be for us — the one thing we keep doing no matter what?
Where do we already have a small habit that's quietly growing something good?

title: Relate — September 2026
coverLines: A door that opened when two people knocked together
Around the family table — one line from each club
Impact — the families we walked with this season
summary: Term 3 in the life of the Relate family: Greentree's doors open, one line from each club, and the people God has been walking with.

blocks.text: Welcome, family. This issue of Relate is about doors — the ones God opens when two people knock on them together, and the ones we keep open for each other all year. Somewhere on every page of this magazine someone has, at some cost, said to a neighbour: you are not alone, come in.
So in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others.

Every club in Relate began with a single yes — someone willing to open a door and invite a family in. This term that story repeats itself across town, where Greentree throws its doors open to the neighbourhood: a place for meals, homework talk, drop-in prayer and the long work of becoming a family.

Two families knocked first. Then three more rang the bell before the paint had dried. A week in, the leaders stopped scheduling and simply started setting extra places at the table — because a door, opened in faith, decides what it is once people walk through.

A verse for your mirror
Wilma practiced, and then she ran
summary: October's study guide for Sprout Kids (6–8): five habits, five weeks, one strong tree — verses, dailies and the story of a girl who practised until she ran.

blocks.text: How to use this study guide

This is a study guide for Sprout Kids families. October has five weeks, so here are five habits to grow — one a week. Each week has a verse to read out loud, a few lines to think about, and a short Try it list. Read together at one meal, keep the verse card on the fridge, and watch a small habit grow a strong tree.

Wilma Rudolph was a little girl who became very sick, and the doctors said she might never walk again. So she got up each day — rain, sun, homework or not — and she practised. Standing. Then stepping. Then walking. Then running, a little more every single day. By the time she grew up, the girl who was not supposed to walk had won three gold medals at the Olympics. She did not win them in one giant leap. She grew them with small habits, repeated daily — until the habit started running for her.

blocks.caption: Small steps, kept daily, become golden runs.

blocks.text: Source: Wilma Rudolph, Wilma (1977); U.S. Olympic & Paralympic Museum biography.

A habit is just a promise you keep until it keeps you. This month we plant five small ones — one verse and one try-it for every week. By the last week of October you will have a tree you grew yourself.
Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the Lord your God will be with you wherever you go.

Your teeth get brushed every morning whether you feel like it or not — because you practised until brushing decided for you. God's words can do the same. Say a verse before your feet hit the floor, so the first word of your day is courage.

blocks.caption: Say it before your feet hit the floor — courage, first thing.

items: Write Joshua 1:9 on a card and tape it to the bathroom mirror
Say it twice while you brush — once for you, once for someone you love
On Friday, teach the verse to someone in your family

blocks.text: Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters.
A made bed is a small door you opened for good things. Tidying your corner is the first thing you get to rule — and the child who rules her own corner can rule a whole school week.

blocks.caption: A corner you rule is a corner you keep.

items: Make your bed every morning this week
Give every toy and book a home, and put it back after play
On Friday, ask a grown-up to look at your space and celebrate it

blocks.text: Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.
Kindness is a habit too. You cannot wait to feel kind — you do the kind thing and the feeling follows. One kind thing a day, repeated, changes the whole mood of a classroom.

blocks.caption: One kind thing, repeated, changes the whole mood of a classroom.

items: One kind thing every day — mark it on a kindness chart
Let someone go first once today
Say thank you to one teacher before Friday

blocks.text: Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established.
School is work, and work loves a routine. The children who seem to do well are rarely the cleverest — they are the ones with boring, beautiful habits: homework first, bags ready, and asking early.

blocks.caption: The school habit: the same time, every day.

items: Homework before screens — the same time every weekday
Pack your bag tonight, not tomorrow morning
The brave question: ask for help in the first week, not the last

blocks.text: Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus.
Thanks is a muscle — like the garden we planted last season, it grows when you water it. Two thanks at dinner, every night, and by Friday the jar is full enough to read out loud.

blocks.caption: Thanks, like a seed, grows when you water it.

items: Start a gratitude jar — any jar will do
Plant a seed this week and water it every day
Name two thanks at dinner each night; read the jar on 31 October

blocks.text: Sprout Kids (6–8): ask a grown-up to read the verse of the week with you at breakfast, then say it back. Your habit for the month is the teeth-and-verse morning — a small, brave start to every day.
Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much.

items: Which girl practised standing when doctors said she never would?
Which young king asked God for wisdom, not treasure?
Finish it: 'Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be…'

blocks.text: Spring has a way of preaching without words. Every seed we pressed into the soil at the Sprout garden day was a small sermon: growth is slow, unseen at first, and unstoppable once it starts. This issue of Rooted is about that kind of growth — in children, in families, and in the quiet volunteers who show up week after week.
Rejoice with those who rejoice; mourn with those who mourn.

The Sprout club opened the season with thirty-two new faces. The Reading Circle's new badge system has children racing to finish their first five books, and the memory-verse board is full for the first time. If you have an hour a week, there is a chair waiting for you.

blocks.text: How to help your child love reading

Literacy volunteers shared three habits that consistently work: let children choose their own books, read aloud together even after they can read alone, and talk about the story at dinner. Ten minutes a day beats an hour once a week.
Children are one third of our population and all of our future.
